> >  Fernanda:
> >
> > It is fine that you have used the characters "M" and "F" in your
> > data.  You can use those as covariates after you have indicated to
> > MCDS that the field does not contain numbers, but rather contains
> > charters you wish to consider as "factors."  Look at the screen
> > capture I will send separately from the project Amakihi that is
> > provided in the Sample Projects folder that comes with program Distance:
> >
> > The covariate "OBs" which are the initials of the observers making the
> > sightings, are indicated to be "factor" variables.  Try this analysis
> > yourself by looking through the Amakihi Distance project.
> >
> > Of course clusters do not have genders, but Distance does not know
> > that.  I suspect it would make your analysis most simple if you were
> > to analyse your data as detections of single individuals (whenever you
> > have sightings of a multi-individual cluster, you duplicate records
> > such that there are as many records (with perpendicular distances
> > equal) as there were animals in the cluster).  Simulations described in
> >
> > Buckland, S.T., Plumptre A.J., Thomas, L. and Rexstad, E.A.. (2010)
> > Design and analysis of line transect surveys for primates
> > <http://www.springerlink.com/content/w975167n11kp8403//>.
> > /International Journal of Primatology/ *31*: 833-847, DOI
> > 10.1007/s10764-010-9431-5
> >
> > provide some justification for treating clusters as groups of individuals.
> >
> >

Thank you so much for writing me back!

I also think that it would be better to analyze my data as single
individuals rather than cluster. But since it wasn't possible to measure
the distance for each individual when a cluster was detected isn't there
any problem to use the same distance for the individuals in the cluster?

measure the distance to each individual in the cluster but I could not do
that in the field because individuals flushed as soon as they were
detected.

Many thanks,

Fernanda Alves.

messages.subject: Re: Accounting for No Observations
messages.body_plain:
Kelly:

You ought to see a row in the data table without data in the
'Observation layer' that corresponds to transects you walked without
registering any sightings.  I will show you a screen capture offline
(Jiscmail does not allow sending attachments) of how your data should
appear inside Distance.

Meanwhile you can look for yourself by opening the sample project
"Stratify example.dst" that can be found in the "Sample Projects"
directory when you open Distance.  Look at transects 5 and 6.

In addition to this you can view a brief description of the data import
process at this web location

http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance.workshops/distance2013/preparingdata.html

showing a transect without sightings (line 1 in stratum 2).

Finally, the URL above also points you to a narrated video that you can
watch and listen to (if you are willing to use a Java plugin on your
computer) demonstrating the data import process.

messages.subject: model selection and large SEs on p
messages.subject_clean: model selection and large SEs on p
messages.body_plain:
Dear list members,

I am analyzing data from a point-count based monitoring program for which=
 distance estimation is part of the field protocol and for which distance=
-detection modeling is to be used to 'correct' count oberservations for i=
mperfect detection. I am dealing with a bunch of species (61 with > 75 de=
tections, but with about 1/4 of them with > 1000 detections) and potentia=
l models (12 for each species with different combinations of key and adju=
stment functions and covariates).  Small sample sizes in some cases (belo=
w 150 or so, suggest that more complicated covariate models; e.g., models=
 with observer effects, where there might be 20 or more observers) may no=
t be appropriate.  Nevertheless, given the number of specie to be conside=
red, as an initial step, I just ran all species-model combinations with a=
 for loop in R using the Distance package. If I look at just the lowest A=
IC models, I get strongest support in most cases for the more complicated=
 covariate models, yet standard errors for one or more scale covaraiates =
in these models can sometimes be wonky (ie very large), suggesting overfi=
tting. And the reported standard errors for 'average p' can sometimes be =
> > 1, which I don't understand. The detection histograms, and predicted p'=
s look reasonable though (although there is often evidence of fewer than =
expected observations at nearest distances). My initial solution was to e=
liminate models with CVs on the mean detection probability > 100% from co=
nsideration. But I don't have any real theoretical or empirical grounds f=
or doing so. Part of the problem is that I can't figure out how the stand=
ard errors of the average detection probability estimates (presumably cal=
culated using eq. 6.50 in the Buckland et al 2004 book) are calculated an=
d how they can be > 1.=20

So, my questions are 1) how can the average detection probabilities be > =
1?, and 2) how might one proceed in a model-selection framework when prec=
ision seems to be low, but for which AIC suggests you have a good model (=
with maybe one or 2 parameters not estimated well, but the rest of which =
look good).

Any insights or suggestions would be appreciated. Thanks!

--

messages.subject_clean: model selection and large SEs on p
messages.body_plain:
James:

I suspect you have fitted a number of models that have not converged=20
(resulting in the 'wonky' standard errors you describe).  I have the=20
suspicion that this automated approach "all species all keys all=20
adjustments all covariates" is too blunt an instrument for the analyses=20
you wish to perform.

As a first step, check to see whether your models have indeed=20
converged.  You may need to increase the value of the "debug.level"=20
argument to see more detail about the optimisation process for your model=
s.

> > I am analyzing data from a point-count based monitoring program for whi=
ch distance estimation is part of the field protocol and for which distan=
ce-detection modeling is to be used to 'correct' count oberservations for=
 imperfect detection. I am dealing with a bunch of species (61 with > 75 =
detections, but with about 1/4 of them with > 1000 detections) and potent=
ial models (12 for each species with different combinations of key and ad=
justment functions and covariates).  Small sample sizes in some cases (be=
low 150 or so, suggest that more complicated covariate models; e.g., mode=
ls with observer effects, where there might be 20 or more observers) may =
not be appropriate.  Nevertheless, given the number of specie to be consi=
dered, as an initial step, I just ran all species-model combinations with=
 a for loop in R using the Distance package. If I look at just the lowest=
 AIC models, I get strongest support in most cases for the more complicat=
ed covariate models, yet standard errors for one or more scale covaraiate=
s in these models can sometimes be wonky (ie very large), suggesting over=
fitting. And the reported standard errors for 'average p' can sometimes b=
e > 1, which I don't understand. The detection histograms, and predicted =
p's look reasonable though (although there is often evidence of fewer tha=
n expected observations at nearest distances). My initial solution was to=
 eliminate models with CVs on the mean detection probability > 100% from =
consideration. But I don't have any real theoretical or empirical grounds=
 for doing so. Part of the problem is that I can't figure out how the sta=
ndard errors of the average detection probability estimates (presumably c=
alculated using eq. 6.50 in the Buckland et al 2004 book) are calculated =
and how they can be > 1.

> >
> > So, my questions are 1) how can the average detection probabilities be =

> > 1?, and 2) how might one proceed in a model-selection framework when pr=
ecision seems to be low, but for which AIC suggests you have a good model=
 (with maybe one or 2 parameters not estimated well, but the rest of whic=
h look good).

> >
